summary: Defines the Delivered-To email header field, which records the address to which a message was actually delivered. That may differ from the addresses in the To or Cc fields, for example because of forwarding or alias handling. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A note on a letter showing which mailbox it really landed in, even if the envelope said something else.

subtitle: Email header field to record delivery addresses

tldr.problem: Email may pass through mailing lists, forwarding, aliasing, and other transformations before reaching a final recipient. The address on the envelope (RCPT TO) may differ from addresses in the To: or Cc: fields, and there may be multiple intermediate addresses. It is hard to track the delivery path or detect loops.
tldr.mechanism: The Delivered-To header field records each address to which a message was actually delivered, in the order of delivery, building a sequence that shows the path the message took.
tldr.outcome: Email systems can now track delivery paths, help detect loops, and analyze what happened to a message as it moved through the infrastructure. It is experimental.

facts.label: Placement
facts.value: At the top of headers (like Received:)

today: RFC 9228 is an Experimental RFC that standardizes the Delivered-To header field format and semantics. The header has been used informally for decades, but lacks a formal specification. This RFC aims to bring wider adoption and interoperability across email systems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Delivered-To header field records the address to which a message was actually delivered. This is different from the To:, Cc:, or Bcc: fields in the message content, which were written by the author and do not change as the message moves through the email system.

In the email transport system, the actual delivery address is provided separately in the SMTP RCPT TO command and might not match any address in the message header fields. For example, a message sent to a mailing list gets delivered to the list's address, not to each member's individual address. Or a message forwarded through an alias gets delivered to the alias, then to the final recipient.

The Delivered-To field provides a standard way to record each address in this sequence, building a chain that shows the delivery path. This is useful for analyzing email traffic, detecting loops, and understanding how a message traveled through the infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of guessing where an email went, the Delivered-To header writes down each address it actually got delivered to, in order. You can read the whole path at the end.

sections.title: The Delivered-To Header Field
sections.content:
The syntax of the Delivered-To header field is simple: the literal Delivered-To: followed by a single email address (addr-spec), then a line break:

Delivered-To: recipient@example.com

When a message is delivered (that is, when responsibility transfers from the Message Handling Service to a recipient's agent), a Delivered-To field SHOULD be added with the address that was used for delivery. If the receiving system applies local mappings or transformations to the address, a separate Delivered-To field SHOULD also be added for the transformed address.

Unlike some other email headers, each Delivered-To field is added at the current top of the message's header list, similar to the trace fields (Received:) specified in SMTP. This preserves the sequence of deliveries with the first (earliest) delivery at the bottom and the final delivery at the top.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is simple: just the word 'Delivered-To:' and an email address. Every time the email is delivered somewhere new, one more line is added to the top of the list.

sections.title: Multi-Delivery Example
sections.content:
Consider a message sent to a mailing list that then forwards to an alias, which finally reaches the recipient at another email provider:

  • Step 1: Message submitted to list@org.example. The list accepts it with Delivered-To: list@org.example.
  • Step 2: List processes the message and forwards it to Recipient-alumn@edu.example. This generates a second Delivered-To header with the new address, placed at the top.
  • Step 3: The alias at edu.example forwards to theRecipient@example.net. A third Delivered-To header is added at the top.

The final message has three Delivered-To fields, one for each delivery step. A recipient reading the message header can see the entire path: the message went through a list, then an alias, then reached the final destination.

This sequence is stable and preserved as the message is forwarded, unlike the Received: header's 'for' clause, which is optional and inconsistently implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: Picture a package with three stickers, each one written when it reached a new mailbox. By reading them top to bottom, you know where it went: first to the list, then to the alias, finally to you.

sections.title: Uses and Loop Detection
sections.content:
The Delivered-To header supports several use cases:

  • Path analysis: Administrators can trace the delivery path to diagnose mail routing issues or understand complex forwarding arrangements.
  • Loop detection: If the same Delivered-To address appears twice in a message, it indicates that the message has entered a delivery loop. For example, if list@org.example appears twice, the message was delivered to that list twice, which should never happen and suggests misconfiguration.
  • Reply-To address inference: When composing a reply, the software can use the Delivered-To address of the original message to infer a better reply address.

However, loop detection using Delivered-To is more precise than counting Received: headers, because Received: headers only record which MTA processed the message, not which final recipient address was used. Many addresses might route through the same MTA.
sections.plainLanguage: If you see the same address twice, the message went in circles. If you need to reply, you can look at which address really got it and reply there. Managers can also see if mail is taking a weird route.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Concerns
sections.content:
The Delivered-To header discloses information about the email infrastructure and about the recipient. It shows the sequence of addresses used for a single recipient, which reveals details about forwarding, aliasing, and internal routing.

This information might be unintentionally disclosed if a recipient manually forwards a message and includes all original headers. A later recipient could then see the original recipient's intermediate addresses, which was not intended to be public.

Additionally, on systems that store a single copy of a message for multiple recipients, supporting Delivered-To while maintaining privacy is challenging, since exposing different recipient addresses to other recipients can be problematic.

The RFC recommends that implementations provide users with the ability to clear or view their Delivered-To history, and that MTA/MDA developers consider the privacy implications before implementing this header.
sections.plainLanguage: The header can leak private information about how you receive mail. If you forward a message, someone else might see all the intermediate addresses. Be careful when sharing emails.
